findings.issue_text: `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:141` — Worker exceptions are caught but the offset is always marked complete in `finally`, committing failed result processing and permanently losing it despite the successful-processing guarantee.

`src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233` — `shutdown()` sets workers' shutdown flags before queues drain, so workers exit after their current items and leave queued items unprocessed; `close()` stops committing first, causing graceful shutdown to lose queued work.

`src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consers/queue_consumer.py:239` — `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` require Python 3.13; on supported earlier runtimes shutdown is ignored, blocked daemon workers remain alive, and worker joins wait their full timeout.

`src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:178` — Queues have no `maxsize`, so `submit()` provides no backpressure and an overproducing sender can accumulate unbounded decoded results and exhaust memory.

`tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:~1880` — The error-handling test waits only 0.2 seconds before asserting no commit even though the commit loop runs every second, so it cannot detect failed-message commits.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:141` — Worker exceptions are caught but the offset is always marked complete in `finally`, committing failed result processing and permanently losing it despite the successful-processing guarantee.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method in queue_consumer.py lines 117-145, the code catches exceptions in the try block but the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(). This means even when processing fails with an exception (line 138-140 logs the error), the offset is still marked as complete. The class docstring at line 227-231 claims 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' but this implementation violates that guarantee - failed messages will have their offsets committed, causing data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233` — `shutdown()` sets workers' shutdown flags before queues drain, so workers exit after their current items and leave queued items unprocessed; `close()` stops committing first, causing graceful shutdown to lose queued work.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown() method in FixedQueuePool (lines 225-237), it first sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown() on queues, then joins workers. The OrderedQueueWorker.run() method (lines 117-143) checks self.shutdown at the start of each loop iteration. If shutdown is set to True while items are still in the queue, the worker will exit after processing its current item without draining remaining queued items. Additionally, close() in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy (lines 339-342) sets shutdown_event and joins commit_thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops the commit loop before all items are processed. This means queued work items could be lost during graceful shutdown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consers/queue_consumer.py:239` — `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` require Python 3.13; on supported earlier runtimes shutdown is ignored, blocked daemon workers remain alive, and worker joins wait their full timeout.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queue_consumer.py` using `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` at line 239 and catching `queue.ShutDown` exception at lines 127 and 135. According to Python documentation, `queue.Queue.shutdown()` method and `queue.ShutDown` exception were added in Python 3.13. If this code runs on Python versions earlier than 3.13 (which is common since 3.13 was released in October 2024), the shutdown() call will raise AttributeError and the ShutDown exception won't exist. This is a real compatibility bug that would cause the shutdown mechanism to fail on supported Python versions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:178` — Queues have no `maxsize`, so `submit()` provides no backpressure and an overproducing sender can accumulate unbounded decoded results and exhaust memory.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 178 in queue_consumer.py, the FixedQueuePool creates queues with `queue.Queue()` without a maxsize parameter. The docstring at line 232 claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but this is false - unbounded queues never fill up. The submit() method at line 195 uses `work_queue.put()` which will never block on an unbounded queue. This means if producers submit faster than workers can process, memory will grow unboundedly. This is a real correctness/resource exhaustion bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:~1880` — The error-handling test waits only 0.2 seconds before asserting no commit even though the commit loop runs every second, so it cannot detect failed-message commits.

adjudication.rationale: The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` at line ~1880 waits for processing to complete, then only sleeps 0.2 seconds before asserting that no commits happened. However, looking at the `_commit_loop` in `queue_consumer.py` (lines 268-286), it runs `self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)` - meaning it only checks for committable offsets every 1 second. The test's 0.2 second wait is insufficient to verify that commits won't happen after error handling. The test could pass spuriously because the commit loop simply hasn't run yet, not because the error handling correctly prevented commits.
